labelProvenance: Synthetic attempt observations. Queries and relevance labels were written by the author, who could see the documents; they are not independently labelled.

observations.summary: The learner forgot to handle an empty array before reading its first element.
An empty string caused an out-of-bounds access because the first character was read without a guard.
The learner now checks for zero elements before accessing the collection.
The learner shrank the sliding window before recording a valid candidate.
Moving the left pointer too soon discarded the best substring before its length was saved.
The learner correctly saved the current window result before removing its leftmost element.
Binary search did not advance the lower bound when the middle element was rejected, causing an infinite loop.
The learner left the search interval unchanged after a failed midpoint check.
Every binary search iteration strictly reduces the remaining interval.
Graph traversal revisited nodes because the learner marked them visited only after exploring neighbours.
A cycle caused repeated recursive calls because a node was not recorded before descending.
The learner marks each graph node before traversing outgoing edges to prevent revisits.
The learner described two nested loops as linear time without accounting for repeated scans.
The learner justified quadratic running time by counting all pairs inspected.
The imported record reports a solved outcome with no code or reflection; no diagnosis is supported.
The learner resized the application window to make the code easier to read.
The learner left the notes field empty after solving the problem.
The loop ran to n inclusive and read one element past the end of the array.
The loop stopped at n minus two, so the final element was never compared.
The learner checked loop bounds against the first and last index before running the code.
3Sum returned repeated triplets because equal values were not skipped after moving the pointers.
After recording a triplet, the learner advanced both pointers past equal values.
A hash set detected whether any value appeared twice, which solved Contains Duplicate.
Two Sum paired an element with itself because it was stored in the map before its complement was looked up.
The learner looked up the complement first and only then stored the current index.
Indices still on the monotonic stack after the scan were never given an answer.
After the final element, the learner assigned the default answer to every index left on the stack.
The learner kept an increasing stack where next greater element needed a decreasing one.
Valid Parentheses popped from an empty stack when a closing bracket came first.
Before matching a closing bracket, the learner confirmed an opening bracket was available on the stack.
Reversing the linked list lost the remaining nodes because next was overwritten before it was saved.
The learner saved the next pointer before redirecting each link during reversal.
Removing the head node needed a separate branch that the learner got wrong.
A sentinel node before the head meant deleting the first node needed no special case.
The fast pointer advanced two steps without checking fast.next, crashing on even-length lists.
Floyd's algorithm checked both fast and fast.next before each double step.
The recursive depth function dereferenced a missing child because there was no base case for None.
The recursion returned zero for an absent child before doing any other work.
The BST check compared each node only with its direct children instead of carrying min and max bounds.
The learner passed lower and upper limits down the recursion to validate every subtree.
Level order traversal mixed nodes from different depths because the queue length was not captured first.
The learner recorded the queue size at the start of each level and processed exactly that many nodes.
The heap grew to all n elements instead of being capped at k, costing n log n.
The learner popped the heap whenever it exceeded k entries.
Backtracking never removed the last choice after recursion, so later branches kept stale elements.
The learner popped the choice after each recursive call to restore the state.
The mutable path list was appended to the results without copying, so every stored result ended up empty.
The learner saved a copy of the current combination rather than the shared list.
Course Schedule never decremented neighbour in-degrees, so no further courses were queued.
Each processed course reduced its neighbours' in-degree, and courses reaching zero were queued.
Flood fill read cells outside the grid because row and column limits were checked after the access.
The learner validated row and column ranges before visiting a neighbouring cell.
Dijkstra processed outdated priority queue entries for nodes whose distance had already improved.
Popped entries with a distance larger than the recorded best were skipped.
Union-find had no path compression or union by rank, so finds degraded to linear chains.
The learner added path compression so repeated find calls stayed nearly constant.
House Robber used dp[i-2] before the first two states were initialised.
The learner set the first two DP entries explicitly before applying the recurrence.
Recursive Climbing Stairs recomputed the same subproblems exponentially without memoization.
The learner cached results by index so each subproblem was solved once.
The longest common subsequence table had no extra row and column, so index minus one went negative.
The learner allocated an (m+1) by (n+1) table so the empty prefix had its own row.
Merge Intervals missed overlaps because the intervals were not sorted by start first.
The learner sorted intervals by start time before merging adjacent ones.
Intervals that shared an endpoint were treated as separate although the problem counted them as overlapping.
Counting set bits right-shifted a negative Python integer, and the loop never ended.
The learner masked the value to 32 bits before counting set bits.
Trie search returned true for a prefix because the end-of-word flag was not checked.
Search returned true only when the final node was marked as the end of a word.
The midpoint was computed as (lo + hi) / 2 in Java, which can overflow.
The learner used lo + (hi - lo) / 2 to avoid integer overflow.
The learner started coding before asking whether the input could contain negative numbers.
The learner asked about value ranges and duplicates before proposing an approach.
The learner jumped to an optimised approach without first stating a simple baseline.
The learner stated a simple baseline solution out loud before looking for a faster one.
The solution was declared finished without tracing an example; the failing case appeared only on submission.
The learner walked through a two-element example by hand before submitting.
An imported attempt has only a date and an outcome, with no code or notes to diagnose.
The learner reviewed a stack of flashcards before the session started.
The editor ran low on heap memory while many browser tabs were open.
The learner drew a graph of weekly practice hours in their notes.
The learner downloaded the binary installer for a new code editor.
The learner reorganised the folder tree that holds their practice files.
Dismissed observation: a note about checking an empty input was a hypothetical reminder, not a reported mistake.

queries.text: Do I forget to guard against collections containing no items?
Am I discarding a valid sliding-window result before saving it?
Does my binary search always make progress?
Do graph cycles cause me to visit the same node repeatedly?
Can I correctly explain the cost of nested iteration?
Which attempt has insufficient evidence for a learning diagnosis?
Do my loop bounds skip the last element or read past the end?
Am I producing repeated triplets by not skipping equal values?
Do I accidentally match a number with itself when looking up its complement?
Do I resolve the items still left on the monotonic stack when the scan ends?
Do I check that the stack has something before popping it?
Do I lose the rest of the list when reversing pointers?
Do I struggle when the first node of a linked list has to be deleted?
Do I guard against null before moving the fast pointer twice?
Do my tree recursions handle missing children?
Am I validating a binary search tree only against immediate children?
Do I keep breadth-first levels of a tree separate?
Do I keep the heap limited to k items?
Do I undo my choice after exploring a backtracking branch?
Do I store a reference to the working path instead of a snapshot?
Do I update in-degrees correctly in topological sort?
Do I check grid boundaries before reading a neighbouring cell?
Do I ignore outdated entries popped in Dijkstra's shortest path?
Do my disjoint-set lookups stay fast?
Do I initialise dynamic programming base cases before the recurrence?
Do I cache overlapping subproblems?
Do I leave room for the empty prefix in a 2-D DP table?
Do I order intervals before merging them?
Do my bit counting loops terminate for negative numbers?
Does my trie tell a complete word apart from a prefix?
Could my midpoint calculation overflow?
Do I clarify input constraints before I start coding?
Do I state a simple solution before optimising?
Do I trace an example by hand before submitting?
